strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important gap: how KV cache compression affects multi-instruction prompts, an underexplored scenario relative to standard single-instruction benchmarks.

Comprehensive empirical study spanning five diverse eviction policies (StreamingLLM, H2O, K-norm, SnapKV, TOVA) across two model families, with consistent methodology (KVPress) that aids reproducibility.
The system-prompt leakage case study is a compelling and concrete illustration of the abstract 'selective amnesia' phenomenon, tying the compression pitfalls to a security-relevant consequence.
Identifies and disentangles two distinct causes of degradation (instruction hardness vs. eviction bias) using a reasonable quantitative tool (Spearman rank correlation across instruction classes).

Proposes two lightweight, clearly specified interventions (manual whitelisting and a formally defined 'fair eviction' policy with an explicit algorithm) and shows they measurably reduce leakage with limited cost to directive-following, providing actionable takeaways for practitioners.
Extensive supplementary figures/ablations (order flipping, kept-token percentages, per-model breakdowns) support the central claims with converging evidence rather than a single anecdote.
weaknesses: Only two base models (Llama3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 14B) are tested; claims about general 'model' dependence (Pitfall 2) rest on a very narrow sample, limiting confidence in generalizability across architectures/scales.

The system-prompt leakage experiments rely on a single templated defense/directive structure (fixed wording, one leakage-eliciting query) and a two-instruction abstraction (X/Y); it is unclear how well this generalizes to more heterogeneous, multi-part real-world system prompts.

No reporting of variance, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing for the accuracy/ROUGE-L curves, despite greedy decoding being used throughout, making it harder to assess whether some fine-grained differences (e.g., slope comparisons across policies) are robust or noise.
ROUGE-L recall is a coarse proxy for 'leakage'; it may over- or under-count genuine semantic disclosure of system instructions, and no human or LLM-judge validation of the leakage metric is provided.

The proposed 'fair eviction' method assumes a priori knowledge of instruction span boundaries (defense vs. directive), which is a strong practical assumption; the paper does not address how boundaries would be identified automatically in deployment, nor how the method scales beyond two spans to prompts with many orthogonal instructions.
Manual whitelisting is acknowledged as ad hoc and reliant on user intuition, reducing its practical scalability as a general solution.

The 'Pitfall' framing (six numbered pitfalls) organizes largely expected observations (non-uniform degradation, method/model dependence, order sensitivity) in a somewhat informal narrative structure rather than a more rigorously derived theoretical account of why specific instruction classes or positions are targeted.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and underexplored topic: how KV cache compression interacts with multi-instruction prompts, using system prompt leakage as a concrete, security-relevant case study.

The experimental design spanning multiple eviction policies (StreamingLLM, H2O, K-norm, SnapKV, TOVA), two models (Llama3, Qwen2), and multiple compression ratios provides reasonably broad coverage for identifying qualitative trends.

The identification of 'eviction bias' (differential eviction rates across co-occurring instructions) and the demonstration that instruction order and defense placement affect leakage rates is an interesting and plausible phenomenon that could inform future eviction policy design.
The proposed fixes (whitelisting and fair eviction) are simple, easy-to-implement, and intuitively motivated by the diagnosed failure mode, providing an actionable mitigation direction.
The paper is generally well organized around a sequence of clearly labeled 'pitfalls,' which aids readability and narrative structure.
weaknesses: Evidence is almost entirely visual/qualitative: nearly all claims rest on reading curve slopes in multi-panel figures without reporting any quantitative statistics, significance tests, confidence intervals, or effect sizes, making it hard to assess robustness of the 'pitfalls.'

The case study is narrow: only two models and a fairly synthetic single defense-prompt template (with fixed wording) and a single leakage query are used; generalizability of findings (e.g., to other model families, scales, or realistic system prompts) is unverified.

Key quantities like 'accuracy' and 'leakage' metrics (ROUGE-L recall) are not benchmarked against human judgment or validated as reliable proxies for actual leakage/instruction-following, raising concerns about construct validity.

The proposed 'fair eviction' and whitelisting solutions are tested only in the same narrow two-instruction (defense+directive) setting that motivated them, so it is unclear they generalize to more than two instructions or arbitrary prompt structures; no comparison against simple baselines (e.g., just increasing budget for system prompts generally, or not compressing short system prompts at all) is provided.

The paper lacks statistical rigor in reporting: no variance across seeds/decoding runs, no sample-size details beyond 541 IFEval prompts, and conclusions about 'order effects' or 'degradation rates' are drawn from eyeballing trends rather than formal comparison.

The fair eviction algorithm requires knowing instruction span boundaries a priori (which instructions exist and where they lie in context), which is a strong assumption that is not discussed as a limitation—undermining the practical applicability of the fix in real deployments where instruction structure may not be known to the serving infrastructure.

The paper's contribution is largely empirical observation plus two very simple heuristic fixes; the fixes do not constitute a new eviction policy design principle validated at scale or compared quantitatively (with numbers) against baselines across many conditions, limiting the technical depth of the contribution.
No discussion of computational cost/overhead of the proposed fair/whitelist methods, nor of how a practitioner would identify multiple instructions or whitelist tokens automatically in practice.

The related work and taxonomy sections, while thorough, occupy significant space without correspondingly deep empirical follow-through, and some pitfalls (e.g., Pitfall 2 on method/model dependence) are fairly unsurprising restatements of known compression trade-offs rather than novel findings.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored blind spot in the KV cache compression literature: most existing evaluations use single-instruction benchmarks, while this paper convincingly shows that multi-instruction prompts (e.g., system prompts with a directive+defense) degrade non-uniformly under compression, with real security implications (prompt leakage).

The empirical investigation is reasonably thorough: five distinct eviction policies (StreamingLLM, H2O, K-norm, SnapKV, TOVA) are evaluated across two models (Llama3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B), multiple compression ratios, and instruction orderings, giving a fairly comprehensive picture of how the phenomenon manifests across the design space.

The paper goes beyond simple observation to provide a mechanistic explanation: by measuring per-instruction 'keep rates,' it convincingly links eviction bias to the observed asymmetric degradation and leakage curves (Figure 8), strengthening the causal story rather than leaving it as correlation.

The non-monotonic leakage curve (rising then falling with compression ratio) is an interesting and non-obvious empirical finding, with a sensible explanation (loss of the leaked content itself at very high compression).

Two simple, practically deployable mitigations (token whitelisting and a formalized 'fair eviction' policy) are proposed and empirically shown to reduce leakage with minimal cost to directive-following accuracy across most eviction methods and both models, giving the paper actionable value for practitioners.
The organization around discrete, clearly labeled 'Pitfalls' makes the contributions easy to follow and cite, and is likely to be useful as a checklist for future compression method designers.
weaknesses: Model coverage is limited to two models (Llama3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B); it is unclear how well the findings (especially the specific bias patterns per eviction method) generalize to other architectures, model families, or much larger/smaller models.

The experimental setup (system prompt + short IFEval-derived instructions) does not clearly reflect the long-context regime in which KV cache compression is most commonly deployed in practice (tens of thousands of tokens); it is unclear whether the eviction-bias effects observed here persist, amplify, or diminish at realistic long-context scales, which somewhat weakens the paper's framing around 'realistic scenarios.'

The system-prompt leakage case study relies on a single, fairly templated defense prompt (fixed wording given in Appendix A) and a single adversarial leakage query; results may be sensitive to prompt phrasing and it is unclear how robust the findings are to more varied/adversarial system prompt designs.

No error bars, variance across seeds, or statistical significance analysis are reported for any of the curves, making it hard to assess how much of the observed slope differences (e.g., in Figures 2–7) reflect noise versus a robust effect.

The proposed 'fair eviction' method assumes known, disjoint instruction spans are available at inference time; this is a nontrivial practical requirement (accurate instruction segmentation) that is not addressed, limiting the immediate deployability of the solution in real serving systems where instruction boundaries may not be cleanly delineated.

Leakage is measured solely via ROUGE-L recall against reference text, which may miss paraphrased or semantically leaked content and could underestimate true leakage in some cases; no human evaluation or complementary semantic-similarity metric is used to corroborate the ROUGE-L based leakage claims.

Whitelisting, while simple, requires manual specification of the tokens to protect, which is an ad hoc solution that does not obviously scale to arbitrary system prompts/instructions without human intervention.

strengths: Identifies a genuinely underexplored and practically important phenomenon: KV cache compression does not degrade instructions uniformly, and this non-uniformity translates into a concrete security vulnerability (system prompt leakage).

Thorough empirical investigation spanning 5 eviction policies (StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV, TOVA, K-Norm) and 2 models (Llama3 8B, Qwen2.5 14B), with multiple complementary analyses (accuracy curves, rank correlation, keep-rate/eviction bias heatmaps, per-layer analysis).

The system-prompt leakage case study is a compelling and realistic framing that connects an efficiency technique to a security concern, which should be of interest to both the efficiency and safety/security communities.

Provides plausible mechanistic explanations (Appendix J) for why each eviction policy exhibits particular biases (e.g., recency bias in StreamingLLM/H2O/SnapKV vs. K-Norm's opposite bias), adding some interpretive depth beyond pure observation.

Extensive validation and robustness checks in appendices: LongBench TREC experiments at multiple context lengths, LLM-as-a-judge leakage evaluation as an alternative to ROUGE-L, runtime/throughput overhead measurements, and a tunable debiasing parameter with Pareto-frontier analysis.

Proposed fixes (whitelisting and fair eviction) are simple, easy to reason about, and show consistent (if modest) improvements across policies and models in Table 1, supporting the paper's diagnostic claims about eviction bias and semantic importance.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to two models (Llama3 8B and Qwen2.5 14B), which the paper itself acknowledges limits generalizability given Pitfall 2's own claim that effects are highly model/policy-dependent; broader model coverage (different scales, architectures, more recent models) would substantially strengthen the claims.

Both proposed mitigations (whitelisting and fair eviction) require a priori, manual knowledge of instruction spans/boundaries and assume instructions are of roughly equal importance and well-formed — a strong assumption that is explicitly flagged as a limitation and restricts practical deployment, especially in the online compression setting that is arguably more relevant to real production systems.

The paper only studies offline compression of a fixed prefix (the system prompt/query), while much real-world KV cache compression is applied online during decoding over unbounded generation; the authors acknowledge this but it limits the direct applicability of the main claims and proposed fixes to realistic deployment scenarios.

Leakage quantification relies primarily on ROUGE-L recall, a fairly coarse lexical-overlap metric that may not robustly capture semantic leakage; although LLM-as-judge validation is included, it is relegated to the appendix and only tested on Llama3, not fully integrated into the main claims.

The improvements from fair eviction/whitelisting, while consistent, are often numerically modest (e.g., several entries in Table 1 around 0.01–0.02), and the practical significance of these gains for real deployment is not clearly contextualized against, e.g., accuracy loss trade-offs a practitioner would care about.

The synthetic defense/directive setup (explicit 'do not reveal instructions' + adversarial 'reveal previous instructions' prompts) is a reasonable but simplified proxy for real system-prompt leakage scenarios; results on more diverse, realistic system prompts (as might arise from deployed commercial assistants) are not shown, which could affect the generality of the leakage findings.

The paper is dense with many individually-flagged 'pitfalls' (1 through 6) without a unifying theoretical framework tying them together, making the contribution feel more like a catalog of empirical observations than a cohesive analytical contribution.

strengths: Addresses an important, understudied problem: how KV cache compression behaves under realistic multi-instruction prompts rather than single-instruction benchmarks, and connects this to a concrete security concern (system prompt leakage).

Reasonably broad empirical coverage: five eviction policies (StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV, TOVA, K-Norm) across two model families/sizes, with a large and varied appendix (LongBench validation, LLM-as-judge alternative to ROUGE-L, runtime/throughput overhead measurements, per-layer keep-rate heatmaps, Pareto-based debiasing analysis).
The 'eviction bias' framing and the keep-rate analysis (Figure 7) provide a clear, well-supported mechanistic account of why leakage occurs, going beyond a purely black-box accuracy plot.

Proposed mitigations (keyword whitelisting, fair eviction) are simple, cheap to implement, and empirically shown to consistently improve the leakage/accuracy trade-off across policies and models (Table 1/2), which gives the paper some practical value for practitioners.
Use of Spearman rank correlation to quantify heterogeneous degradation, and the single- vs multi-instruction comparison, is a sensible and interpretable methodological choice.
weaknesses: Several of the six 'pitfalls' are fairly predictable restatements of the same underlying phenomenon (uneven eviction hurts some instructions more) rather than independent, surprising findings; the paper's framing inflates the apparent number of contributions.

The explanatory account of *why* different eviction policies exhibit bias (Appendix J) is explicitly hypothesis-driven ('we speculate', 'we attribute this to') and is not rigorously validated with targeted ablations, weakening the causal story behind the central claims.

Fair eviction and whitelisting both require a priori knowledge of instruction spans/keywords, restricting applicability to offline, well-segmented prompts; the authors' own limitations section concedes this does not extend cleanly to online compression, which is arguably the more latency-critical deployment setting the paper motivates in the introduction.

The proposed 'fair eviction' fix is a fairly simple proportional budget-allocation heuristic rather than a new eviction mechanism grounded in attention/semantics; for K-Norm, scores are literally left unchanged (Appendix F.6), suggesting the fairness adaptation is somewhat superficial for embedding-based methods.
The equal-weighting score in Section 6 (0.5 accuracy + 0.5 leakage) is an arbitrary utility function with no sensitivity analysis or justification for why practitioners would value the two equally.

Experiments rely on synthetic, author-constructed defense/directive templates (Appendix B) rather than real-world deployed system prompts, which limits ecological validity of the leakage numbers and the generality of the 'critical compression ratio' claims.

Model coverage (Llama3 8B, Qwen2.5 14B) is narrow for a paper making general claims ('KV cache compression leads to system prompt leakage' as a blanket pitfall); no larger or differently-architected models (e.g., MoE, different attention variants) are tested in the main text.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: the interaction between KV cache compression and multi-instruction prompting, with a compelling security angle (system prompt leakage) that connects efficiency research to safety/robustness concerns.

Comprehensive empirical scope: five distinct eviction policies (position-, attention-, embedding-, and hybrid-based) evaluated on two model families, with systematic ablations on instruction order, compression ratio, and eviction bias.

The paper builds a coherent causal narrative across the 'pitfalls' (non-uniform degradation → eviction bias → order sensitivity → leakage), each substantiated with quantitative evidence (normalized accuracy curves, Spearman rank correlation, keep-rate/eviction bias plots).

Proposed mitigations (token whitelisting and fair eviction) are simple, easy to implement on top of existing policies, and empirically shown to consistently improve the leakage/accuracy trade-off (Table 1) at negligible decoding overhead (Appendix K).

Extensive robustness checks in the appendix (LongBench/TREC generalization, LLM-as-judge leakage metric as alternative to ROUGE-L, per-layer eviction analysis, Pareto-optimal debiasing sweep) substantially strengthen confidence in the main findings and reproducibility.
Clear and well-organized presentation with a useful taxonomy of eviction methods and a concrete formalization of 'fair eviction' that could be adopted by other researchers.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to two model families (Llama3 8B, Qwen2.5 14B); while this is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation, it leaves open how well the eviction-bias phenomenon and proposed fixes generalize to other architectures/scales (e.g., MoE models, models with different attention-sink behavior).

The defense/directive system-prompt leakage setup is a synthetic construction (via Mu et al. 2025 template) rather than real-world deployed system prompts, and the 'leakage' metric (ROUGE-L recall against reference text) is a coarse proxy for actual information disclosure, though this is partly mitigated by the LLM-as-judge appendix experiment.

Whitelisting and fair eviction, while effective, are manual/heuristic interventions that require prior knowledge of instruction spans; the paper explicitly defers automation to future work, somewhat limiting the immediate practical impact of the proposed solutions.

The explanations for why particular eviction policies favor recent vs. early tokens (Appendix J) are largely post-hoc and speculative ('we hypothesize', 'we speculate') rather than rigorously validated, which weakens the mechanistic understanding offered for Pitfall 5/6.

Some of the main claims (e.g., Pitfall 1 that instructions degrade unevenly) are somewhat expected given known properties of position- and attention-based eviction; the paper's novelty lies more in the systematic characterization and mitigation than in a fundamentally new phenomenon.
